content:
I’d like to share graphql-lean, a Lean 4 formalization of GraphQL, based on the September 2025 specification. An earlier Coq formalization of the 2018 GraphQL specification, the GraphCoQL project, did not model several important parts of the execution semantics, including the @skip and @include directives, non-null types, and execution errors. My Lean formalization covers most of the constructs needed to state GraphQL execution semantics.

I think this is an interesting industrial use case for Lean. With help from LLMs, I translated the English specification into Lean and reviewed the LLM-generated definitions. My rough estimate is that current frontier models get them about 90% right on the first attempt. The LLMs and I then iteratively refined the definitions as theorem development exposed problems. I’m now reasonably confident that they are faithful to the specification within the project’s stated scope.

I wrote three accompanying blog posts with more detailed explanations:

  • Formalizing GraphQL and Proving Query Normalization in Lean
  • When GraphQL Normalization Does Not Preserve Validation
  • Executing GraphQL Without CollectFields

Feedback is very welcome. Most of the project was written by LLMs, and I did not manually review the proofs. Once I was satisfied with the definitions and theorem statements, I let Lean’s kernel check the rest. :) I suspect this will become a common mode of Lean usage.

Notification Bot said:

This topic was moved here from #Project announcements > graphql-lean: New GraphQL Formalization in Lean by Michael Rothgang.

Well, I don't consider this is an AI authored project. I reviewed the definitions and theorem statements line by line and edited them heavily. AI simply couldn't get it done satisfactorily by itself. Only the proofs are solely authored by AI. I believe all projects would (should) be AI-assisted to some degree now.

Daniil Iaitskov said:

How much tokens have been spent?

Unfortunately, I don't have exact token accounting. I used my personal ChatGPT Pro subscription. I've been working on this for a month-ish with about half-time effort on my end.

Although many proofs are done with one query, some normalization proofs took 4 hours or more for ChatGPT 5.4 with a few interaction with me. The hardest one was the normal form uniqueness theorem, which took 2 weeks for GPT 5.4 to prove with a lot of interaction with me.
I'm inclined to agree that this didn't need to be moved.

In my opinion,

Most of the project was written by LLMs, and I did not manually review the proofs.

qualifies for inclusion in this channel.

Michael Rothgang said:

In my opinion,

Most of the project was written by LLMs, and I did not manually review the proofs.

qualifies for inclusion in this channel.

I do think hand-curated proofs have their own place. We need proof theories and techniques developed.

I see 3 categories of projects.

  • Theorems where proof themselves are interesting. This is the main interests in Lean channel.
  • AI-proved projects where only specifications are human written or reviewed.
  • AI moonshot projects (no human author)

The title of this channel suggested the 3rd category ("AI authored" can be misunderstood.), but now I understand both 2 and 3 fall in this channel after all.
